rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem type is a compressed, read-only Linux filesystem embedded in small systems. A cramfs image can be used without prior decompression of the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem type is a free version of the Veritas filesystem type. It is the primary filesystem type for HP-UX operating systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs file system type is a hierarchical file system that allows mounting of Mac OS file systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem designed to replace hfs and allowing Mac OS filesystems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 file system type (Journalling Flash File System 2) is a log-structured file system used on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs file system type is a compressed, read-only Linux file system embedded in small-footprint systems. A squashfs image can be used without first unpacking the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf file system type is the Universal Disk Format used to implement the ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 specifications. It is an open-vendor file system type for storing data on a wide range of media. This file system type is required to support DVD writing and newer optical disc formats.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The USB storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: A USB drive provides a means to transfer and store files, ensuring their persistence and availability regardless of network connectivity. Its popularity and usefulness have led to USB-based malware becoming a simple and common means of penetrating a network and a first step toward establishing a persistent threat in the network environment.
rules.impact: Restricting USB access on the system will reduce the physical attack surface of the device and reduce possible malware introduction vectors.

rules.title: Unused filesystem kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: File system kernel modules are pieces of code that can be dynamically loaded into the Linux kernel to extend file system capabilities of the so-called operating system base kernel. File system kernel modules are typically used to add support for new hardware (as device drivers) or to add system calls.
rules.impact: Although loadable filesystem kernel modules are a convenient method of modifying a running kernel, attackers can abuse them on a compromised system to hide their processes or files, allowing them to retain control of the system. Many rootkits use loadable filesystem kernel modules in this way. Removing support for unnecessary filesystem types reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it. The following filesystem kernel modules have CVEs and should be made unavailable if no dependencies exist: • afs — CVE-2022-37402 • ceph — CVE-2022-0670 • cifs — CVE-2022-29869 • exfat CVE-2022-29973 • ext CVE-2022-1184 • fat CVE-2022-22043 • fscache CVE-2022-3630 • Fuse CVE-2023-0386 • gfs2 CVE-2023-3212 • nfs_common CVE-2023-6660 • nfsd CVE-2022-43945 • smbfs_common CVE-2022-2585

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications. IF an entry for /tmp exists in /etc/fstab, it takes precedence over entries in the default systemd unit file. Note: In an environment where the primary system is diskless and attached via iSCSI, entries in /etc/fstab may not take precedence. /tmp can be configured to use tmpfs. tmpfs places everything in the kernel's internal caches, grows and shrinks to accommodate the files it contains, and can swap unnecessary pages out to swap space. It has maximum-size limits that can be adjusted on the fly with the mount -o remount command. Because tmpfs resides entirely in the page cache and swap, all tmpfs pages are shown as "Shmem" in /proc/meminfo and "Shared" in free. Note that these counters also include shared memory. The most reliable way to obtain a count is to use df and du. tmpfs has three mount options to define size: • size: the limit of allocated bytes for this tmpfs instance. The default is half of physical RAM without swap. If you exceed the size of tmpfs instances, the machine will lock up because the OOM handler will be unable to free that memory. • nr_blocks: Same as size, but in PAGE_SIZE blocks. • nr_inodes: the maximum number of inodes for this instance. The default is half the number of pages of physical memory, or (on a highmem machine) the number of lowmem RAM pages, whichever is smaller. These parameters accept a k, m, or g suffix and can be changed on remount. The size parameter also accepts a % suffix to limit this tmpfs instance to that percentage of physical RAM. By default, if neither size nor nr_blocks is specified, size=50% is used. Page 68
rules.impact: Creating a dedicated file system for /tmp allows the administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, which makes /tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It will also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link would be broken and the attacker would have their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were discovered in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability. This can be done either by mounting tmpfs on /tmp or by creating a separate partition for /tmp.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/fstab or in systemd unit file tmp.mount

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot execute binaries from /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is world-writable and can function as shared memory facilitating inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Creating /dev/shm as its own file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, which makes /dev/shm useless to an attacker for installing executable code. It will also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a setuid system program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link will be broken and the attacker will have their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were found in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability. This can be done by mounting tmpfs on /dev/shm.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /dev/shm file system is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create special devices on /dev/shm partitions.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the filesystem prevents users from installing privileged programs on the system and allowing non-root users to execute them.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the filesystem prevents users from executing programs from shared memory. This deters users from introducing potentially malicious software into the system.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to satisfy local users' disk space needs.
rules.impact: By default, only a single / partition is created. Because the /home directory contains user-generated data, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. Essentially, the entire disk is available to be filled, affecting the system as a whole. In addition, other operations on the system may fill the disk independently of /home and affect all local users. Configuring /home as its own file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system. For /home, options such as usrquota/grpquota can be considered to limit the impact users can have on each other with respect to disk resource exhaustion. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details of file-system-independent and file-system-specific options. Because /home contains user data, care should be taken to protect the security and integrity of the data and the mount point.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /home partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /home.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /home partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is intended only for storing user files, set this option to ensure that users cannot create setuid files in /home.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be world-writable.
rules.impact: The reasons for placing /var on a separate partition are as follows. By default, only a single / partition is created. Because the /var directory may contain world-writable files and directories, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. Essentially, the entire disk is available to be filled, affecting the system. In addition, other operations on the system may fill the disk independently of /var and lead to unexpected system-wide behavior because the disk is full. See man auditd.conf for details. Configuring /var as a separate file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details of file-system-independent and file-system-specific options. An example of exploiting /var would be an attacker creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link may be broken, and the attacker will obtain their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were found in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var file system is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications. Temporary files in /var/tmp should persist across reboots.
rules.impact: A default installation creates only a single / partition. Because the /var/tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. In addition, other operations on the system can fill a disk unrelated to /var/tmp and cause potential disruption of daemons because the disk is full. Configuring /var/tmp as a separate file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot create setuid files in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot execute binaries from /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: A default installation creates only one / partition. Because the /var/log directory contains log files that can become quite large, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. In effect, it would have the entire disk available to fill and affect the system as a whole. Configuring /var/log as a separate file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit the ability of attackers to create exploits on the system. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details of file-system-independent and file-system-specific options. Because /var/log contains log files, care should be taken with the security and integrity of the data and the mount point.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is intended only for log files, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is intended only for log files, set this option to ensure that users cannot execute binary files from /var/log.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The Auditd daemon stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: A default installation creates only a single / partition. Because the /var/log/audit directory contains the audit.log file, which can grow to a very large size, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. In effect, the entire disk will be available to fill and impact the system as a whole. In addition, other operations on the system may fill the disk unrelated to /var/log/audit and cause auditd to initiate its space_left_action when the disk is full. See man auditd.conf for details. Configuring /var/log/audit as a separate filesystem allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details on filesystem-independent and filesystem-specific options. Because /var/log/audit contains audit logs, care should be taken with the security and integrity of the data and the mount point.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit file system is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option to ensure that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is intended only for audit logs, set this option to ensure that users cannot execute binaries from /var/log/audit.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM package manager implements GPG key signing to verify package integrity during and after installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that updates are obtained from a valid source to protect against spoofing, which could result in the unintentional installation of malware on the system. To do this, ensure that GPG keys are configured correctly for your system.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/yum.repos.d/*, /etc/dnf/dnf.conf; GPG keys in /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/

rules.title: Gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck parameter, located in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and in individual /etc/yum.repos.d/* files, determines whether the RPM package signature is verified before installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the RPM package signature is always verified before installation to guarantee that the software is obtained from a trusted source.

rules.title: Repo_gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The repo_gpgcheck parameter, located in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and individual /etc/yum.repos.d/* files, will perform GPG signature verification of repository data.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the repository data signature is always verified before installation to guarantee that the software will not be tampered with in any way.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems should have appropriate package manager repositories configured to ensure that the system can receive the latest patches and updates.
rules.impact: If system package repositories are configured incorrectly, important patches may not be identified, or a rogue repository may contain compromised software.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: Patches are periodically released for installed software either due to security flaws or to enable additional functionality.
rules.impact: Newer patches may contain security improvements that will not be available in the latest full update. For this reason, it is recommended to use the latest software patches to take advantage of the newest features. As with any software installation, organizations need to determine whether a given update meets their requirements and verify compatibility and supportability of any additional software with the selected update version.
rules.scope: Update parameters: dnf check-update, installed packages

rules.title: SELinux is installed
rules.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control.
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system installed, only the default discretionary access control system will be available.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: SELinux is enabled at boot and is not overridden by GRUB boot parameters.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot in your GRUB configuration to ensure that the controls it provides will not be overridden.

rules.title: The SELinux policy is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux matches or exceeds the default targeted policy, which restricts only daemons and system software.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary from site to site. Some sites may require a more restrictive policy than the default, which is acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that at least the default recommendations are met.

rules.title: SELinux mode is not disabled
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing: • Enforcing — the default and recommended operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux operates normally, applying the loaded security policy to the entire system. • Permissive — the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including object labeling and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but it does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful when developing SELinux policy. • Disabled — strongly discouraged; the system not only avoids enforcing SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, making it more difficult to enable SELinux in the future. Note: You can set individual domains to permissive mode while the system is running in enforcing mode. For example, to make the httpd_t domain permissive: # semanage permissive -a httpd_t
rules.impact: Running SELinux in disabled mode is strongly discouraged; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy but also avoids labeling any persistent objects, such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult. Page 154

rules.title: SELinux mode is enforcing
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing: • Enforcing — the default and recommended operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux operates normally, applying the loaded security policy to the entire system. • Permissive — the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including object labeling and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but it does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful when developing SELinux policy. • Disabled — strongly discouraged; the system not only avoids enforcing SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, making it more difficult to enable SELinux in the future. Note: You can set individual domains to permissive mode while the system is running in enforcing mode. For example, to make the httpd_t domain permissive: # semanage permissive -a httpd_t
rules.impact: When running SELinux in disabled mode, the system not only avoids enforcing SELinux policy but also avoids labeling any persistent objects, such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult. Running SELinux in permissive mode, although useful for SELinux policy development, only logs access denial entries but does not deny any operations.

rules.title: Unrestricted services do not exist
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined domains
rules.impact: Unconfined processes are subject to SELinux policy rules, but there are policy rules that allow processes running in unconfined domains nearly all access. Processes running in unconfined domains fall back to using DAC rules exclusively. If an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux does not prevent an attacker from accessing system resources and data, but DAC rules are still applied. SELinux is a security enhancement in addition to DAC rules, but it does not replace them.

rules.title: The MCS translation service (mcstrans) is not installed
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon provides category label information to client processes that request it. Label translations are defined in /etc/selinux/targeted/setrans.conf.
rules.impact: Because this service is used infrequently, remove it to reduce the amount of potentially vulnerable code executing on the system.

rules.title: SETroubleshoot is not installed
rules.explanation: The SETroubleshoot service notifies desktop users of SELinux denials through a user-friendly interface. The service provides important information about configuration errors, unauthorized intrusions, and other potential errors.
rules.impact: The SETroubleshoot service is an unnecessary daemon started on a server, especially if X Windows is disabled.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password will require anyone who reboots the system to enter a password before they can set boot parameters from the command line.
rules.impact: Requiring a boot password when the bootloader runs prevents an unauthorized user from entering boot parameters or modifying the boot partition. This prevents users from weakening security (for example, disabling SELinux at boot).
rules.scope: Settings in file user.cfg in directory /boot/grub2/

rules.title: Access to the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: GRUB files contain boot configuration information and passwords for unlocking boot options.
rules.impact: Setting read and write permissions for the root user only prevents non-root users from viewing or modifying boot parameters. Non-root users who read boot parameters may discover security weaknesses at boot time and exploit them.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit-mitigation technique that randomly distributes the address space of key process data areas.
rules.impact: Random placement of virtual memory regions will make it more difficult to write exploits against memory pages, because memory placement will constantly change.

rules.title: Ptrace_scope is restricted
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call provides a means by which one process (the "tracer") can observe and control the execution of another process (the "tracee"), and also inspect and modify the memory and registers of the traced object.
rules.impact: If a single application is compromised, an attacker will be able to attach to other running processes (for example, Bash, Firefox, SSH sessions, the GPG agent, and so on) to obtain additional credentials and continue expanding the scope of the attack. Enabling restricted mode will limit a compromised process's ability to use PTRACE_ATTACH on other processes running under the same user. In restricted mode, ptrace will continue to work for the root user.

rules.title: Kernel dump tracing is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program terminated abnormally. It can also be used to obtain sensitive information from a core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken at the moment the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is typically useful only to developers attempting to troubleshoot issues, increasing risk to the system.

rules.title: Kernel dump storage is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program terminated abnormally. It can also be used to obtain sensitive information from a core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image captured when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is typically useful only to developers attempting to debug issues.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set to a legacy version
rules.explanation: If a system-wide policy is configured, default application behavior will follow that policy. Applications will not be able to use algorithms and protocols that do not comply with the policy unless you explicitly request the application to do so. System-wide crypto policies followed by core cryptographic components allow algorithms to be consistently deprecated and disabled system-wide. The LEGACY policy provides maximum compatibility with operating system version 5 and earlier; it is less secure due to an increased attack surface. In addition to DEFAULT-level algorithms and protocols, it includes support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1. DSA, 3DES, and RC4 algorithms are allowed, and RSA keys and Diffie-Hellman parameters are accepted if their length is at least 1023 bits.
rules.impact: If the system-wide LEGACY crypto policy is selected, it includes support for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and SSH2 or later. DSA, 3DES, and RC4 algorithms are allowed, and RSA and Diffie-Hellman parameters are accepted if their length is greater than 1023 bits. These legacy protocols and algorithms can make the system vulnerable to attacks, including those listed in RFC 7457.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set in the sshd configuration
rules.explanation: The system-wide cryptographic policy can be overridden or disabled for OpenSSH.
rules.impact: Overriding or opting out of system-wide crypto policy may allow less secure ciphers, MACs, KexAlgorithms, and GSSAPIKexAlgorithm to be used. Note: If changes to system-wide crypto policy are required to meet local site policy for the OpenSSH server, those changes should be made using a subpolicy assigned to the system-wide crypto policy. For additional information, see the CRYPTO-POLICIES(7) man page.

rules.title: The system-wide encryption policy disables SHA1 hash and signature support
rules.explanation: SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm) is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit hash value.
rules.impact: The SHA-1 hash function has a weak design, and advances in cryptanalysis have made it vulnerable to attacks. The most serious risk to a hashing algorithm is a collision, which occurs when two different pieces of data produce the same hash value. This hashing algorithm has been considered weak since 2005. Note: Use of SHA-1 with Hash-based Message Authentication Codes (HMAC) does not depend on the collision resistance of the underlying hash function, so recent attacks on SHA-1 have significantly less impact on SHA-1 used for HMAC. For this reason, this recommendation does not disable the hmac-sha1 MAC.

rules.title: The system-wide encryption policy disables Mac computers with a key size of less than 128 bits
rules.explanation: A message authentication code (MAC) algorithm is a family of cryptographic functions parameterized by a symmetric key. Each function can act on variable-length input data (called a "message") to produce an output value of a specified length. The output value is called the MAC of the input message. A MAC algorithm can be used to provide data origin authentication and data integrity protection.
rules.impact: Weak algorithms continue to attract significant attention as a weakness that can be exploited as computational power increases. An attacker who breaks the algorithm can use a MiTM position to decrypt the tunnel and obtain credentials and information. A MAC algorithm must make it computationally infeasible to determine the MAC of a message without knowledge of the key, even if one has already seen the results of using that key to compute MACs of other messages.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables cbc for SSH
rules.explanation: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) is an algorithm that uses a block cipher.
rules.impact: There is a vulnerability in SSH messages that use CBC mode that may allow an attacker to recover plaintext from a ciphertext block. If exploited, this attack could potentially allow an attacker to recover up to 32 bits of plaintext from an arbitrary ciphertext block from a connection protected with the SSH protocol.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables chacha20-poly1305 for ssh
rules.explanation: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithm that combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 message authentication code. Its use in IETF protocols is standardized in RFC 8439.
rules.impact: A vulnerability exists in ChaCha20-Poly1305 as documented in CVE-2023-48795. Page 206.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables EtM for ssh
rules.explanation: Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM). Ciphertext is generated by encrypting plaintext and then appending a MAC of the encrypted plaintext.
rules.impact: There is an effective attack against the use of SSH Cipher-Block-Chaining (CBC) with Encrypt-then-MAC, as described in CVE-2023-48795.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and serve as a message of the day for authenticated users. Unix-based systems typically display OS version and patch-level information at login. This information can be useful to developers developing software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty(8) supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m — computer architecture \r — operating system version \s — operating system name \v — operating system version
rules.impact: Warning banners inform users attempting to log in of their legal status with respect to the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any existing monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to exploit specific system vulnerabilities. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging in. Page 214

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before login on local terminals. Unix-based systems typically display OS version and patch-level information at login. This information can be useful to developers developing software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty(8) supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m — computer architecture \r — operating system version \s — operating system name \v — operating system version — or the operating system name

Displaying OS and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to exploit specific system vulnerabilities. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging in.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured services. Unix-based systems typically display OS version and patch-level information at logon. This information can be useful to developers developing software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty(8) supports the following parameters, they display operating system information: \m — computer architecture \r — operating system version \s — operating system name \v — operating system version

Displaying OS and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to exploit specific system vulnerabilities. rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and act as a message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: - IF - /etc/motd is not configured with correct access, it can be modified by unauthorized users using incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on at local terminals.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue.net file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The GNOME display manager is removed
rules.explanation: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) is a program that manages graphical display servers and handles graphical user login.
rules.impact: If a graphical user interface (GUI) is not required, it should be removed to reduce the system attack surface.

rules.title: The GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME display manager that provides graphical logon for GNOME-based systems.
rules.impact: Warning banners inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any existing monitoring policies.

rules.title: The GDM disabled user list option is enabled
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME Display Manager, which provides graphical logon for GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list setting controls whether the user list is displayed on the logon screen.
rules.impact: Displaying a user list eliminates half of the username-and-password equation that an unauthorized person would need to log on to the system.

rules.title: The GDM screen is locked when the user is idle
rules.explanation: GNOME Desktop Manager can automatically lock the screen when a user is idle for a period of time. • Idle-delay=uint32 {n} — the number of seconds of idle time before the screen blanks. • lock-delay=uint32 {n} — the number of seconds after the screen blanks before the screen is locked. Example key file: # Specify the dconf path [org/gnome/desktop/session] # Number of seconds of idle time before the screen blanks # Set to 0 seconds if you want to disable the screensaver. Idle-delay=uint32 900 # Specify the dconf path [org/gnome/desktop/screensaver] # Number of seconds after the screen blanks before locking the screen lock-delay=uint32 5
rules.impact: Setting a lockout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access by a user to another user's unattended session.

rules.title: GDM screen lock cannot be overridden
rules.explanation: GNOME Desktop Manager can automatically lock the screen when a user has been idle for some time. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings. To lock a dconf key or subpath, create a locks subdirectory in the keyfile directory. Files inside this directory contain a list of keys or subpaths to lock. As with keyfiles, you can add any number of files to this directory. Example lock file: # Lock screensaver desktop settings /org/gnome/desktop/session/idle-delay /org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/lock-delay
rules.impact: Setting a lock value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access by a user to another user's unattended session. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings. Page 243

rules.title: GDM automounting of removable media is disabled
rules.explanation: By default, GNOME automatically mounts removable media when inserted for user convenience.
rules.impact: If automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and access its contents on the system, even if they do not have permission to mount it themselves.

rules.title: The GDM setting that disables automatic mounting of removable media is not overridden
rules.explanation: By default, GNOME automatically mounts removable media when it is inserted as a convenience for the user. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings. To lock a dconf key or subpath, create a locks subdirectory in the keyfile directory. Files in this directory contain a list of keys or subpaths to lock. As with keyfiles, you may add any number of files to this directory. Example lock file: # Lock automount settings /org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/automount /org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/automount-open
rules.impact: If automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and access its contents on the system, even if they do not have permission to mount it themselves.

rules.title: GDM autorun is never enabled
rules.explanation: The autorun-never parameter allows the GNOME Display Manager to disable autorun via GDM.
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can exploit AutoRun features when the media is inserted into the system and launched.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never is not overridden
rules.explanation: The autorun-never setting allows the GNOME Desktop Display Manager to disable autorun through GDM. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings. To lock a dconf key or subpath, create a locks subdirectory in the keyfile directory. Files in this directory contain a list of keys or subpaths to lock. As with keyfiles, you may add any number of files to this directory. Example lock file: # Lock desktop media-handling settings /org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/autorun-never
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can take advantage of AutoRun features when the media is inserted into the system and launched. Page 262

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: The X Display Manager Control Protocol (XDMCP) is intended to provide authenticated access to display manager services for remote displays.
rules.impact: XDMCP is inherently insecure. • XDMCP is not an encrypted protocol. This may allow an attacker to intercept keystrokes entered by the user. • XDMCP is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. This may allow an attacker to steal legitimate users' credentials by impersonating the XDMCP server.

rules.title: Autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs automatically mounts devices, typically including CD/DVD and USB drives.
rules.impact: If automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and access its contents on the system, even if they do not have permission to mount it themselves.

rules.title: Avahi daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a multicast DNS/DNS-SD service discovery system. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on a local network without special configuration. For example, a user can connect a computer to the network and Avahi automatically finds printers to print to, files to browse, people to communicate with, and network services running on the computer.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is generally not required for system operation. It is recommended to remove this package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: DHCP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a service that allows machines to be assigned IP addresses dynamically. There are two versions of the DHCP protocol: DHCPv4 and DHCPv6. At startup the server can be started for one or the other using the -4 or -6 arguments.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically configured to operate as a DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the dhcp-server package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: DNS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical naming system that maps names to IP addresses of computers, services, and other resources connected to the network.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended to operate as a DNS server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight tool that provides DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) services.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended as a DNS cache, DNS forwarder, and/or DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share file systems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise file systems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and file systems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this package can be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Ftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Message access server services are not used
rules.explanation: dovecot and cyrus-imapd are open-source IMAP and POP3 server packages for Linux-based systems.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. Note: There are several IMAP/POP3 servers that may use other service names. Those should also be reviewed and the packages removed if they are not required.

rules.title: Network file system services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most widely used file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides systems the ability to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not require access to shared network resources or the ability to provide Network File System services for shared network resources on other hosts, it is recommended to remove the nfs-utils package to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: NIS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Network Information Service (NIS), formerly known as "Yellow Pages", is a client-server directory service protocol used to distribute system configuration files. The NIS client (ypbind) was used to bind a computer to an NIS server and obtain the distributed configuration files.
rules.impact: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks and buffer overflows and has weak authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has typically been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended that the service be removed.

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Common Unix Printing System (CUPS) provides the ability to print to both local and network printers. A system running CUPS can also accept print jobs from remote systems and print them on local printers. It also provides the ability to administer the service remotely via the web.
rules.impact: If the system is not required to print jobs or accept print jobs from other systems, it is recommended to remove CUPS to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on. RPC processes notify rpcbind at startup, registering the ports they listen on and the RPC program numbers they intend to serve. A client system then contacts rpcbind on the server with a specific RPC program number. rpcbind.service redirects the client to the correct port number so it can contact the requested service. Portmapper is an RPC service that always listens on TCP and UDP 111 and is used to map other RPC services (such as nfs, nlockmgr, quotad, mountd, and so on) to the corresponding port number on the server. When a remote host makes an RPC call to this server, it first consults the port map to determine where the RPC server is listening.
rules.impact: A small request (~82 bytes over UDP) sent to Portmapper generates a large response (amplification from 7x to 28x), making it a suitable tool for DDoS attacks. If rpcbind is not required, it is recommended to remove the rpcbind package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsyncd.service service can be used to synchronize files between systems over network links.
rules.impact: If not required, the rsync-daemon package should be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. The rsyncd.service poses a security risk because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.

rules.title: Snmp services are not used
rules.explanation: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is a widely used protocol for monitoring the status and health of network equipment, computer hardware, and devices such as UPS units. Net-SNMP is a suite of applications used to implement SNMPv1 (RFC 1157), SNMPv2 (RFC 1901–1908), and SNMPv3 (RFC 3411–3418) over both IPv4 and IPv6. Support for classic SNMPv2 (also known as "historic SNMPv2" — RFC 1441–1452) was discontinued in version 4.0 of the UCD-snmp package. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP commands from an SNMP management system, execute commands or collect information, and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: An SNMP server may communicate using SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and does not require authentication to execute commands. SNMPv3 replaces the simple/cleartext password exchange used in SNMPv2 with more securely encoded parameters. If the SNMP service is not required, the net-snmp package should be removed to reduce the system's attack surface. Note: If SNMP is required: • The server should be configured for SNMP v3 only. User authentication and message encryption must be configured. • If SNMP v2 is absolutely necessary, change the community string values.

rules.title: Telnet server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow a user who can monitor network traffic to steal credentials. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and a higher level of security.

rules.title: TFTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a TFTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to gain access to files.

rules.title: Web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically configured to operate as a proxy server, it is recommended that the squid package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. Note: There are several HTTP proxy servers. They should be reviewed and removed if not needed.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers provide the ability to host website content.
rules.impact: If there is no locally approved requirement to run a web server service on the system, web server packages should be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Extended InterNET Daemon (xinetd) is an open-source super-daemon that replaced the original inetd daemon. The xinetd daemon listens for known services and dispatches the appropriate daemon to respond to service requests.
rules.impact: If xinetd services are not required, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the system's attack surface. Note: If an xinetd service or services are required, ensure that all unnecessary xinetd services are stopped and masked.

rules.title: X Window Server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface (GUI) in which users can have multiple windows to run programs and various add-ons. The X Window System is typically used on workstations where users log on, but not on servers where users typically do not log on.
rules.impact: If your organization does not specifically require graphical login access via X Windows, remove it to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs), such as sendmail and Postfix, are used to listen for incoming mail and deliver messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If the system is not intended to operate as a mail server, it is recommended to configure the MTA to process local mail only.
rules.impact: Mail transfer agent software is complex, and most MTAs have a long history of security issues. Although it is important to ensure that the system can process local mail, there is no need for the MTA daemon to listen on a network port unless the server is intended to operate as a mail server that receives and processes mail from other systems. Page 329

rules.title: Only approved services listen on the network interface
rules.explanation: A network port is identified by its number, the associated IP address, and the communication protocol type, such as TCP or UDP. A listening port is a network port that an application or process listens on, acting as a communication endpoint. Each listening port can be opened or closed (filtered) by a firewall. In general terms, an open port is a network port that accepts incoming packets from remote locations.
rules.impact: Services listening on the system present a potential risk as an attack vector. These services should be reviewed, and if they are not required, the service should be stopped and the package containing the service should be removed. If required packages have dependencies, the service should be stopped and masked to reduce the system attack surface.

rules.title: The fTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or authentication credentials. If file transfer is required, it is recommended to use SFTP. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The ldap client is not installed
rules.explanation: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a method of looking up information in a central database.
rules.impact: If the system will not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended to remove the software to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The nis client is not installed
rules.explanation: The Network Information Service (NIS), formerly known as "Yellow Pages", is a client-server directory service protocol used to distribute system configuration files. The NIS client (ypbind) was used to bind a computer to an NIS server and obtain the distributed configuration files.
rules.impact: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks and buffer overflows and has weak authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has typically been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended that the service be removed.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and increased security and is included in most Linux distributions.

rules.title: The tftp client is not installed
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: Time synchronization is used
rules.explanation: System time should be synchronized across all systems in the environment. This is typically done by establishing an authoritative time server or set of servers and synchronizing all systems to them. Note: If another time synchronization method is used, this section may be skipped.
rules.impact: Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos, and also ensures that log files have consistent timestamps across the enterprise, which aids forensic investigations.

rules.title: Chrony is configured
rules.explanation: chrony is a daemon that implements the Network Time Protocol (NTP) and is designed to synchronize system clocks across various systems and to use a high-accuracy source. Additional information about chrony can be found at http://chrony.tuxfamily.org/. chrony can be configured as a client and/or a server.
rules.impact: If Chrony is used on the system, correct configuration is essential to ensure that time synchronization operates properly.

rules.title: Chrony is not started as the root user
rules.explanation: The /etc/sysconfig/chronyd file allows chrony parameters to be configured, including the user under which chrony is started. By default this is the chrony user.
rules.impact: Services must not run as the root user.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon is used to run batch jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that must run, and cron is used to execute them.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/crontab are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to manage its own jobs. The commands in this item ensure that root is the user and group owner of the file and that only the owner can access the file.
rules.impact: This file contains information about which system jobs are executed by cron. Write access to these files can give unprivileged users an opportunity to escalate their privileges. Read access to these files can give users insight into system jobs that run on the system and an opportunity to obtain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.hourly are configured
rules.explanation: This directory contains system cron jobs that must be run hourly. Files in this directory cannot be managed with the crontab command; they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing unprivileged users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users may give them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory may give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.daily are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that need to run daily. Files in this directory cannot be managed with the crontab command; instead, they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users may give them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory may give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.weekly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run weekly. Files in this directory cannot be managed with the crontab command; instead, they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users may give them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory may give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.monthly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run monthly. Files in this directory cannot be managed with the crontab command; instead, they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the root user and group, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users may give them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory may give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.d are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that should run similarly to the hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but require more granular control over when they run. Files in this directory cannot be managed with the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor. The commands below restrict read/write and search access to the user and group root, preventing ordinary users from accessing this directory.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users may give them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory may give an unprivileged user insight into how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: crontab is the program used to install, remove, or list the tables used to drive the cron daemon. Each user may have their own crontab, and although these are files in /var/spool/cron/crontabs, they are not intended to be edited directly. If the /etc/cron.allow file exists, you must be listed in it (one user per line) to be allowed to use this command. If /etc/cron.allow does not exist but /etc/cron.deny exists, you must not be listed in /etc/cron.deny in order to use this command. If neither of these files exists, then depending on site-specific configuration parameters, only the superuser will be allowed to use this command, or all users will be able to use this command. If both files exist, /etc/cron.allow takes precedence. This means /etc/cron.deny is ignored, and your user must be listed in /etc/cron.allow in order to use crontab. Regardless of whether either of these files exists, the administrative root user is always allowed to configure crontab. The /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny files, if they exist, must be either world-readable or readable by the crontab group. If they are not, cron will deny access to all users until the permissions are corrected. There is one file per user crontab in the /var/spool/cron/crontabs directory. Users are not permitted to edit files in this directory directly, to ensure that only users the system has allowed to run periodic tasks can add them, and that only syntactically correct crontabs are written there. This is enforced by making the directory writable only by the crontab group and by setting the crontab command setgid to that specific group. Note: • Even if a given user is not listed in cron.allow, cron jobs can still be run as that user. • The /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny files, if they exist, control only administrative access to the crontab command for scheduling and modifying cron jobs.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule cron jobs. Using the cron.allow file to control who can run cron jobs enforces this policy. An allow list is easier to manage than a deny list. With a deny list, you could potentially add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.

rules.title: At is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at command allows fairly complex time specifications, extending the POSIX.2 standard. It accepts time in HH:MM format to run a job at a specified time of day. (If that time has already passed, the next day is assumed.) You can also specify midnight, noon, or teatime (4:00 p.m.), and specify a time of day with an AM or PM suffix to run in the morning or evening. You can also specify the day on which the job will run by giving a date in month-name day format with an optional year, or by specifying a date in MMDD[CC]YY, MM/DD/[CC]YY, DD.MM.[CC]YY, or [CC]YY-MM-DD format. The date specification must follow the time-of-day specification. You can also specify a time such as "now" + count time-units, where the time units may be minutes, hours, days, or weeks, and you can specify that the job run today by adding the suffix "today" to the time, and run the job tomorrow by adding the suffix "tomorrow" to the time. The files /etc/at.allow and /etc/at.deny determine which users may submit commands for later execution via at or batch. The file format is a list of usernames, one per line. Spaces are not allowed. If /etc/at.allow exists, only the usernames listed in it are permitted to use at. If /etc/at.allow does not exist, /etc/at.deny is checked, and every username not mentioned in it is permitted to use at. An empty /etc/at.deny file means that every user may use at. If neither file exists, only the superuser may use at.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule jobs. Using the at.allow file to control who can run jobs enforces this policy. An allow list is easier to manage than a deny list. With a deny list, you could potentially add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files. Page 373

rules.title: The IPv6 status is defined
rules.explanation: Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) is the most recent version of the Internet Protocol (IP). It is designed to provide IP addressing and additional security to support the projected growth in the number of connected devices. IPv6 is based on 128-bit addressing and can support 340 undecillion, which is 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456 unique addresses. IPv6 features: • Hierarchical addressing and routing infrastructure • Stateful and stateless configuration • Quality of Service (QoS) support • An ideal protocol for neighbor-node interaction
rules.impact: IETF RFC 4038 recommends developing applications with dual stack in mind. It is recommended to enable IPv6 and configure it according to the recommendations. - IF dual stack and IPv6 are not used in your environment, IPv6 can be disabled to reduce the system's attack surface, and recommendations specific to IPv6 can be skipped. Note: It is recommended to enable and configure IPv6 unless this conflicts with local site policy.

rules.title: Wireless interfaces are disabled
rules.explanation: Wireless networking is used when wired networks are unavailable.
rules.impact: IF wireless is not used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology standard used to exchange data between devices over short distances. It uses UHF radio waves in the ISM bands from 2.402 GHz to 2.48 GHz. It is primarily used as an alternative to wired connections.
rules.impact: An attacker may find a way to access or damage your data. One example of this kind of activity is bluesnarfing, which refers to attackers using a Bluetooth connection to steal information from your Bluetooth device. In addition, viruses or other malicious code may use Bluetooth technology to infect other devices. If you are infected, your data may be damaged, compromised, stolen, or lost.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport-layer protocol that supports multimedia streaming and telephony. DCCP provides the ability to obtain congestion control without implementing it at the application layer, but it does not provide in-order delivery.
rules.impact: IF the protocol is not required, drivers should not be installed in order to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The Tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Transparent Inter-Process Communication (TIPC) protocol is designed to provide connectivity between cluster nodes.
rules.impact: - IF - the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module by disabling the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Reliable Datagram Sockets (RDS) protocol is a transport-layer protocol designed to provide low-latency, high-throughput communication between cluster nodes. It was developed by Oracle Corporation.
rules.impact: - IF - the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module by disabling the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport-layer protocol used to support message-oriented communication with multiple message streams in a single connection. It performs the same function as TCP and UDP, combining features of both. It is message-oriented like UDP and provides reliable, in-order message transport with congestion control like TCP.
rules.impact: - IF - the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module by disabling the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Ip forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding flags are used to tell the system whether it may forward packets.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces (for example, a hard proxy) can never forward packets and therefore will never function as a router.

rules.title: Packet redirect sending is disabled
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. Because the host itself does not act as a router (in a host-only configuration), there is no need to send redirects.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects to other router devices in an attempt to disrupt routing and provide users access to a system configured by the attacker rather than a valid system.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses to 1 prevents the kernel from logging bogus responses (not conforming to RFC-1122) from broadcast frames, preventing filesystems from being filled with useless log messages.
rules.impact: Some routers (and some attackers) send responses that violate RFC-1122 and attempt to fill the log file system with large numbers of useless error messages.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 1 will cause the system to ignore all ICMP echo requests and timestamps to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo requests and timestamps with broadcast or multicast addresses for your network can be used to cause your host to start (or participate in) a Smurf attack. A Smurf attack is based on an attacker sending a large number of broadcast ICMP messages with a spoofed source address. All hosts that receive this message and respond will send echo replies back to the spoofed address, which is likely unroutable. If many hosts reply to the packets, the volume of traffic on the network can increase significantly.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and instruct your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This mechanism allows an external routing device to update your system's routing tables.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This is a way to allow an external routing device to update your system's routing tables. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects, net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects, net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept any ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except they originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are most likely safe.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table updates from possibly compromised known gateways.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 forces the Linux kernel to use reverse path filtering for a received packet to determine whether the packet is valid. Essentially, with reverse path filtering, if the return packet does not leave from the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 is a good way to prevent attackers from sending your system spoofed packets that cannot be answered. One case where this feature does not work is when asymmetric routing is used. This can occur when using dynamic routing protocols (bgp, ospf, and so on) on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: On a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. In contrast, non-source-routed packets follow a path determined by routers in the network. In some cases systems may be unreachable or inaccessible from some locations (for example, private addresses or Internet-routable), so source-routed packets will need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route, net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route, net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system from accepting source-routed packets. Assume that this system is capable of routing packets to Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another interface. Assume that the private addresses do not support routing to Internet-routable addresses and vice versa. Under normal routing circumstances, an attacker using Internet-routable addresses cannot use the system as a means of accessing private-address systems. However, if source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to private-address systems because the route could be specified rather than relying on routing protocols that would not permit such routing.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged
rules.explanation: If this feature is enabled, packets with non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log.
