rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians and net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians to 1 enables this feature. Logging these packets allows the administrator to investigate the possibility that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
rules.explanation: If tcp_syncookies is set, the kernel will process TCP SYN packets normally until the half-open connection queue fills, after which SYN cookie functionality takes effect. SYN cookies work by not using the SYN queue at all. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN/ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses, port number, and the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to allow the connection even if there is no corresponding SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN flood attacks to deny service to the targeted system by sending many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This rapidly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents successful connections. Setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 1 enables SYN cookies, allowing the system to continue accepting valid connections even when a denial-of-service attack is occurring.

rules.title: Ipv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send Router Advertisement messages to announce their availability and convey information to neighboring nodes, allowing them to autoconfigure on the network. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra determine the system's ability to accept these advertisements.
rules.impact: It is recommended that systems not accept router advertisements, because they can be tricked into redirecting traffic to compromised machines. Setting static routes within the system (typically a single default route to a trusted router) protects the system from incorrect routes. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra to 0 disables the system's ability to accept IPv6 router advertisements.

rules.title: Nftables is installed
rules.explanation: nftables provides a new in-kernel packet classification framework based on a network-specific virtual machine (VM) and a new userspace command-line tool, nft. nftables reuses existing Netfilter subsystems, such as the existing hook infrastructure, connection tracking, NAT, the userspace queueing subsystem, and logging.
rules.impact: nftables is a Linux kernel subsystem that can protect against threats originating from the corporate network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host.

rules.title: A single firewall configuration utility is in use
rules.explanation: Using a single effective firewall configuration utility is critical to Linux security. Firewalls act as digital gatekeepers, filtering network traffic based on rules. Proper firewall configuration ensures that only legitimate traffic is processed, reducing the system's exposure to potential threats. The choice between FirewallD and NFTables depends on the organization's specific needs: FirewallD is a firewall service daemon that provides a dynamically managed host-based firewall with a D-Bus interface. Being dynamic, it allows rules to be created, modified, and deleted without restarting the firewall daemon each time rules change. NFTables includes the nft utility for configuring the Linux kernel nftables subsystem. Notes: • firewalld with the nftables backend does not support passing custom nftables rules into firewalld using the --direct option. • To configure firewall rules for nftables, a firewall utility must be installed and active on the system. Using more than one firewall utility can produce unexpected results. • Port 22 (ssh) must be updated to allow connections only from systems that require SSH access, in accordance with site policy.
rules.impact: Proper configuration of a single firewall utility minimizes cyber threats and protects services and data while avoiding vulnerabilities such as open ports or exposed services. Standardizing on a single tool simplifies management, reduces errors, and improves the security of Linux systems. Page 470

rules.title: Firewalld removes unnecessary services and ports
rules.explanation: Services and ports may be accepted or explicitly rejected or dropped by a zone. For each zone you can set default behavior that will handle incoming traffic that is not otherwise specified. This behavior is defined by setting the zone target. There are three options: default, ACCEPT, REJECT, and DROP. • ACCEPT — you accept all incoming packets except those denied by a specific rule. • REJECT — you deny all incoming packets except those allowed by specific rules, and the originating host is informed of the rejection. • DROP — you deny all incoming packets except those allowed by specific rules, and no information is sent to the originating host. Note: • - IF NFTables is used, this recommendation may be skipped. • Port 22 (ssh) must be updated to allow connections only from systems that require SSH connectivity, in accordance with site policy.
rules.impact: To reduce the system attack surface, all unused services and ports should be blocked unless required.

rules.title: Firewalld loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: The loopback interface accepts traffic, and all other interfaces deny traffic to the loopback network.
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the computer and is typically critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen. All other interfaces should ignore traffic for this network as a spoofing protection measure.

rules.title: Nftables base chains exist
rules.explanation: Chains are containers for rules. There are two kinds: base chains and regular chains. A base chain is the entry point for packets from the network stack; a regular chain can be used as a jump target and is used to better organize rules. Note: IF Firewalld is used, this recommendation can be skipped.
rules.impact: If a base chain with a hook for input, forward, and drop does not exist, packets that would pass through these chains will not be affected by nftables.

rules.title: Nftables established connections are configured
rules.explanation: Firewall rules cover new outbound and established connections. Note: If firewalld is used, this recommendation may be skipped.
rules.impact: If rules for established connections are missing, all packets will be dropped by the default policy, preventing network use.

rules.title: Nftables has a default deny firewall policy
rules.explanation: The base chain policy is the default verdict applied to packets that reach the end of the chain.
rules.impact: There are two policies: accept (default) and drop. If the policy is set to accept, the firewall will accept any packet for which a deny is not configured, and the packet will continue through the network stack. It is easier to explicitly allow acceptable use than to deny unacceptable use. Note: • IF Firewalld is used, this recommendation may be skipped. • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system.

rules.title: Nftables loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: The loopback interface accepts traffic, and all other interfaces deny traffic to the loopback network.
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the computer and is typically critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen. All other interfaces should ignore traffic for this network as a spoofing protection measure.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and files ending in .conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory contain configuration specifications for sshd.
rules.impact: sshd configuration specifications must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users. Page 499

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host private key files are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH private key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In this authentication method, possession of the private key is proof of identity. Only the private key that corresponds to the public key will authenticate successfully. Private keys must be stored and handled carefully; copies of private keys must not be distributed.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the SSH host private key file, the host may be impersonated.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In this authentication method, the public key can be used to verify digital signatures created with the corresponding private key. Only the public key that corresponds to the private key will successfully authenticate.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised. Page 506

rules.title: Sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the ciphers that SSH can use during communication. Notes: • Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved ciphers. • ensure that the ciphers in use comply with site policy. • The only "strong" ciphers currently compatible with the FIPS 140 standard are: o aes256-gcm@openssh.com o aes128-gcm@openssh.com o aes256-ctr o aes192-ctr o aes128-ctr.
rules.impact: Weak ciphers used for authentication in a cryptographic module cannot provide confidentiality or integrity, and system data may be compromised. • Triple DES ciphers used in SSH have a birthday bound of approximately four billion blocks, which makes it easier for remote attackers to recover plaintext data via a birthday attack against a long-lived encrypted session, also known as a Sweet32 attack. • Error handling in the SSH protocol; when the client and server use a block cipher algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, it is easier for remote attackers to recover certain plaintext data from an arbitrary ciphertext block in an SSH session through unknown vectors. Page 510

rules.title: Sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: Key exchange is any cryptographic method by which two parties exchange cryptographic keys, enabling use of a cryptographic algorithm. If the sender and receiver wish to exchange encrypted messages, each must be equipped to encrypt outgoing messages and decrypt incoming messages. Notes: • Kex algorithms have higher priority the earlier they appear in the list • Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved key-exchange algorithms • ensure that the key-exchange algorithms in use comply with site policy • The only key-exchange algorithms currently approved under FIPS 140 are: o ecdh-sha2-nistp256 o ecdh-sha2-nistp384 o ecdh-sha2-nistp521 o diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 o diffie-hellman-group16-sha512 o diffie-hellman-group18-sha512 o diffie-hellman-group14-sha256
rules.impact: Key exchange methods that are considered weak should be removed. A key exchange method may be weak because too few bits are used or the hashing algorithm is considered too weak. Using weak algorithms can expose connections to man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: Sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the types of MAC algorithms that SSH can use during communication. Notes: • Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved MACs. • ensure that the MACs in use comply with site policy. • The only "strong" MACs currently approved under FIPS 140 are: o HMAC-SHA1 o HMAC-SHA2-256 o HMAC-SHA2-384 o HMAC-SHA2-512
rules.impact: MD5 algorithms and 96-bit MACs are considered weak and have been shown to increase exploitability in SSH downgrade attacks. Weak algorithms still attract significant attention as a weakness that can be exploited with increased computing power. An attacker who breaks the algorithm can abuse a MiTM position to decrypt the SSH tunnel and obtain credentials and information. Page 518

rules.title: Sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: There are several options for restricting which users and groups can access the system via SSH. It is recommended to use at least one of the following parameters: • AllowUsers: o The AllowUsers variable gives the system administrator the ability to allow specific users to connect to the system via SSH. The list consists of usernames separated by spaces. Numeric user identifiers are not recognized with this variable. If the system administrator wants to further restrict user access by allowing only authorized users from a specific host to log in, the entry can be specified in the form user@host. • AllowGroups: o The AllowGroups variable gives the system administrator the ability to allow specific user groups to connect to the system via SSH. The list consists of group names separated by spaces. Numeric group identifiers are not recognized with this variable. • DenyUsers: o The DenyUsers variable gives the system administrator the ability to deny specific users from logging in via SSH. The list consists of usernames separated by spaces. Numeric user identifiers are not recognized with this variable. If the system administrator wants to further restrict user access by specifically denying a user access from a specific host, the entry can be specified in the form user@host. • DenyGroups: o The DenyGroups variable gives the system administrator the ability to deny specific user groups from logging in via SSH. The list consists of group names separated by spaces. Numeric group identifiers are not recognized with this variable.
rules.impact: Restricting the number of users who can obtain remote access to the system via SSH will help ensure that only authorized users have access to the system. Page 522

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents should be sent to the remote user before authentication is allowed. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users about the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before a user's normal login can help hold attackers accountable on a computer system. Page 526

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: Note: To clarify: the two settings described below apply only to idle connections from a protocol perspective and are not intended to check whether a user is active. An idle user does not mean an idle connection. SSH does not, and never has, provided a capability to intentionally disconnect idle users. In SSH versions prior to 8.2p1 there was a bug that caused these values to behave in a way that was abused to disconnect idle users. That bug was fixed in version 8.2p1, and therefore can no longer be abused to disconnect idle users. The two options ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control the SSH session timeout. Taken directly from man 5 sshd_config: • ClientAliveInterval Sets a timeout interval in seconds after which, if no data has been received from the client, sshd(8) will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response from the client. The default is 0, indicating that these messages will not be sent to the client. • ClientAliveCountMax Sets the number of client alive messages that may be sent without sshd(8) receiving any messages from the client. If this threshold is reached while sending client alive messages, sshd will disconnect the client, terminating the session. It is important to note that the use of client alive messages is very different from TCPKeepAlive. Client alive messages are sent over the encrypted channel and therefore cannot be spoofed. The TCP Keepalive option enabled by TCPKeepAlive can be spoofed. The client alive mechanism is useful when the client or server depends on knowing when a connection has become unresponsive. The default is 3. If ClientAliveInterval is set to 15 and ClientAliveCountMax is left at the default, unresponsive SSH clients will be disconnected after approximately 45 seconds. Setting ClientAliveCountMax to zero disables connection termination. Page 529
rules.impact: To prevent resource exhaustion, appropriate values must be set for both ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax. In particular, looking at the source code, ClientAliveCountMax must be greater than zero in order to use SSH's ability to disconnect idle connections. If connections are allowed to remain open indefinitely, this could potentially be used as a DDoS attack or simple resource exhaustion over unreliable networks. In the example given here, the timeout is 45 seconds. Review your site policy regarding network timeouts and apply it accordingly.

rules.title: Sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding option disables all forwarding features, including X11, ssh-agent(1), TCP, and StreamLocal. This option overrides all other forwarding-related options and can simplify a restricted configuration. • X11Forwarding provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic through the connection to enable remote graphical connections. • ssh-agent is a program for holding private keys used for public key authentication. Through the use of environment variables, the agent can be located and automatically used for authentication when logging in to other machines using ssh. • SSH port forwarding is an SSH mechanism for tunneling application ports from client to server or from servers to clients. It can be used to add encryption to legacy applications, pass through firewalls, and some system administrators and IT specialists use it to open backdoors into the internal network from their home computers.
rules.impact: X11 forwarding is disabled unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that the remote X11 servers of users logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding may be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note: even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always install their own forwarding servers. Anyone with root privileges on an intermediate server can freely use the ssh-agent to authenticate to other servers. Leaving port forwarding enabled may expose the organization to security threats and backdoors. SSH connections are protected by strong encryption. This makes their contents invisible to most deployed network monitoring and traffic-filtering solutions. That invisibility carries significant risk potential if used for malicious purposes such as data theft. Cybercriminals or malware may use SSH to hide unauthorized communications or to steal data from the target network. Page 532

rules.title: Sshd GSSAPI authentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter specifies whether GSSAPI-based user authentication is permitted.
rules.impact: Allowing GSSAPI authentication via SSH exposes the system's GSSAPI to remote hosts and should be disabled to reduce the system attack surface.

rules.title: Sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted.
rules.impact: Although .rhosts files are ineffective if support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: Sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH.

rules.title: Sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication on the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more open unauthenticated connections may exist. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a small value for the LoginGraceTime parameter will minimize the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It will also limit the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections. The recommended value is 60 seconds (1 minute), but set this value in accordance with site policy.

rules.title: Sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: SSH provides several logging levels with different degrees of verbosity. DEBUG options are specifically not recommended except solely for debugging SSH communications. These levels provide so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information and may violate user privacy.
rules.impact: INFO is the baseline level at which only SSH user login activity is recorded. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logout record can exclude users who have disconnected, which helps narrow the field. VERBOSE indicates that login and logout activity will be recorded, as well as the key fingerprint for any SSH key used to log in. This information is important for SSH key management, especially in legacy environments.

rules.title: Sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts allowed for a single connection. When the number of failed login attempts reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the failed login attempts will be written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting a small value for MaxAuthTries will minimize the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. The recommended value is 4, but set this number according to site policy.

rules.title: Sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxStartups parameter specifies the maximum number of concurrent unauthenticated connections to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service due to a large number of pending authentication connection attempts, use the MaxStartups rate-limiting feature to protect sshd login availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxSessions parameter specifies the maximum number of open sessions allowed for this connection.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service due to a large number of concurrent sessions, use the MaxSessions rate-limiting feature to protect sshd login availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits login to accounts with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote access to accounts with empty passwords reduces the likelihood of unauthorized system access.

rules.title: Sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user may log in via SSH. The default is prohibit-password.
rules.impact: Disallowing root logon over SSH requires system administrators to authenticate using their individual accounts and then elevate to root. This provides non-repudiation and a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.

rules.title: Sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to provide environment options to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path that causes SSH to execute Trojan programs).

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this enables PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM option is set to "yes", PAM correctly handles account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at login or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy. The real (not effective) user ID of the calling user is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.
rules.impact: sudo supports a plugin architecture for security policy and I/O logging. Third parties can develop and distribute their own policy and I/O logging plugins to work seamlessly with the sudo interface. The default security policy is sudoers, which is configured via the /etc/sudoers file and any entries in /etc/sudoers.d. The security policy determines what privileges (if any) a user has to run sudo. The policy may require users to authenticate with a password or another authentication mechanism. If authentication is required, sudo will terminate if the user password is not entered within a configurable timeout. This restriction is policy-dependent.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal (pseudo-pty).
rules.impact: Attackers can use sudo to launch a malicious program that will spawn a background process that remains even after the main program finishes executing.

rules.title: The sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: The default log file entry sets the path to the sudo log file. Setting the path enables file logging; negating this option disables it. By default, sudo logs through the system log.
rules.impact: Defining a dedicated log file for sudo simplifies auditing of sudo commands and creating audit rules for sudo.

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users are required to enter a password to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to extend functionality, it is critical that the user reauthenticates.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege elevation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users can reauthenticate to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to extend functionality, it is critical that the user reauthenticates.

rules.title: The sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: sudo caches used credentials for 5 minutes by default. This is done for usability when multiple administrative tasks must be performed. The timeout can be changed in accordance with local security policy.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged access as another user.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in the /etc/pam.d/su file, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead allows system administrators to better control user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: The latest pam version is installed
rules.explanation: Updated PAM versions include additional features.
rules.impact: pam-1.5.1-19 or later is required to provide full system functionality and access to the options covered by this benchmark.

rules.title: The latest version of authselect is installed
rules.explanation: Authselect is a utility that simplifies user authentication configuration. Authselect offers ready-made profiles that can be used universally with all modern identity management systems. You can create and deploy a custom profile by configuring one of the default profiles: sssd, winbind, or nis. This is especially useful if changes to a ready-made authselect profile are not sufficient for your needs. When a custom profile is deployed, it is applied to every user who logs on to the given host. This is the recommended method so that existing profiles remain unmodified. Updated versions of authselect include additional features.
rules.impact: Authselect simplifies testing and troubleshooting because it only modifies files in the following directories: • /etc/nsswitch.conf • /etc/pam.d/* • /etc/dconf/db/distro.d/* To ensure full system functionality and access to the parameters covered by this check, authselect-1.2.6-2 or later is required.

rules.title: The latest version of libpwquality is installed
rules.explanation: libpwquality provides common functions for checking password quality and scoring passwords based on their apparent randomness. The library also provides a function for generating random passwords with good pronounceability. This module can be stacked in the password stack of a given service to enforce password strength checks. The code was originally based on the pam_cracklib module, and this module is backward compatible with its options.
rules.impact: Strong passwords reduce the risk of brute-force compromise.

rules.title: The active authselect profile includes pam modules
rules.explanation: A custom profile can be created by copying and configuring one of the default profiles. Default profiles include: sssd, winbind, and nis. These profiles can be configured to meet the requirements of a specific site. You can select an authselect utility profile for a specific host. The profile will be applied to every user who logs on to the host.
rules.impact: Configuring many pam parameters requires a custom profile. Changes made to the default profile may be overwritten during an update. When you deploy a profile, it is applied to every user who logs on to the given host.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock.so module maintains a list of failed authentication attempts for each user during a specified interval and locks the account if the number of consecutive failed authentications exceeds the configured value (this is determined by the Deny parameter in the Faillock configuration). It stores failure records in per-user files in the Tally directory.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks against your systems.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module performs password quality checking. This module can be stacked in the password stack of a given service to enforce password strength checking. The code was originally based on the pam_cracklib module, and this module is backward compatible with its options. The action of this module is to prompt the user for a password and check its strength against the system dictionary and a set of rules to identify poor choices. The first action is to prompt for a single password, check its strength, and then, if it is considered strong, prompt for the password a second time (to ensure it was entered correctly the first time). If all is well, the password is passed to subsequent modules to be set as the new authentication token.
rules.impact: Using unique and complex passwords increases the time and resources required to compromise a password.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_history.so module stores the last passwords for each user to enforce password-change history and prevent the user from changing the same password too frequently.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_unix.so module is the standard Unix authentication module. It uses standard calls from system libraries to retrieve and set account information and to authenticate. This is typically obtained from the /etc/passwd file and the /etc/shadow file if shadow is enabled.
rules.impact: Requiring users to authenticate reduces the likelihood that an attacker can gain access to the system.

rules.title: Lockout is configured after a failed password entry
rules.explanation: The Deny=<n> option denies access if the number of consecutive failed authentication attempts for this user in the last interval exceeds the limit.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks against your systems.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: unlock_time=<n> - Access will be restored after a number of seconds following lockout. A value of 0 has the same meaning as never: access will not be restored without resetting faillock records using the faillock(8) command. Notes: • The default directory used by pam_faillock is typically cleared at system boot, so access will also be re-enabled after a system reboot. If this is undesirable, a different directory must be set with the dir parameter. • Permanently locking users is generally undesirable because they can easily become the target of a denial-of-service attack unless usernames are random and kept secret from potential attackers. • The maximum configurable value for unlock_time is 604800.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks against your systems.

rules.title: Failed password attempts lockout includes the root account
rules.explanation: Even_deny_root — the root account can be locked in the same way as regular accounts. root_unlock_time=n — this option implies the Even_deny_root option. Allow access to the root account n seconds after the account is locked. If the option is not specified, the value is the same as for the unlock_time option.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks against your systems.

rules.title: The number of changed password characters is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality difok parameter specifies the number of characters in a password that must not be present in the old password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity or strength is a measure of how effectively a password resists guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it will take to crack. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tried before the password is compromised. Page 615

rules.title: Password length is configured
rules.explanation: minlen is the minimum allowed length of a new password (plus one if credits are not disabled, which is the default). It cannot be set below 6.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from brute-force attacks. Page 619

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity can be set using: • minclass — the minimum number of character classes required in a new password (digits, uppercase, lowercase, and other). For example, minclass = 4 requires digits, uppercase and lowercase letters, and special characters. • dcredit — Maximum credit for digits in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of digits in the new password. For example, dcredit = -1 requires at least one digit. • ucredit — Maximum credit for uppercase characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of uppercase characters in the new password. For example, ucredit = -1 requires at least one uppercase character. • ocredit — Maximum credit for other characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of other characters in the new password. For example, ocredit = -1 requires at least one special character. • lcredit — Maximum credit for lowercase characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of lowercase characters in the new password. For example, lcredit = -1 requires at least one lowercase character.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from brute-force attacks. Page 623

rules.title: Passwords with consecutive identical characters are configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxrepeat option sets the maximum number of identical consecutive characters allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity or strength is a measure of how effectively a password resists guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it will take to crack. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tried before the password is compromised. Page 627

rules.title: The maximum number of consecutive password characters is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxsequence option sets the maximum length of monotonic character sequences in a new password. Examples of such a sequence are 12345 or Fedcb. The check is disabled if the value is 0. Note: Most such passwords will fail a simplicity check unless the sequence is only a minor part of the password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity or strength is a measure of how effectively a password resists guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it will take to crack. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tried before the password is compromised. Page 631

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The pwquality dictcheck option determines whether words from the Cracklib dictionary are checked.
rules.impact: If the operating system allows users to choose passwords based on dictionary words, it increases the likelihood of password compromise by increasing the chance of successful guessing and brute-force attacks. Page 635

rules.title: Password quality is required for the root user
rules.explanation: If the pwquality enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will return an error on a failed check even if the user changing the password is the root user. By default this option is disabled, which means that only a message about the failed check is printed, but root can still change the password. Note: Root is not prompted for the old password, so checks comparing the old and new password are not performed.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity or strength is a measure of how effectively a password resists guessing attempts and brute-force attacks. Password complexity is one of several factors that determine how long it will take to crack. The more complex the password, the more possible combinations must be tried before the password is compromised. Page 639

rules.title: Password history remembering is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be checked to ensure that users do not reuse recent passwords. The number of remembered passwords is set using the Remember argument for the pam_pwhistory module. • Remember=<N> — <N> is the number of old passwords that must be remembered.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password. Note: These changes apply only to accounts configured on the local system.

rules.title: Password history is required for the root user
rules.explanation: If the pwhistory Enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will also apply password history for the root user.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password. Note: These changes apply only to accounts configured on the local system.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok — during a password change, force the module to set the new password to the one provided by a previously stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default action of pam_unix.so, which denies a user access to a service if their official password is empty.
rules.impact: Using a strong password is necessary to protect personal and confidential information from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The Remember=n argument stores the n most recent passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd to enforce password change history and prevent a user from changing to the same password too frequently. The MD5 password hashing algorithm is used to store old passwords. The pam_pwhistory module should be used instead of this option. The pam_pwhistory module stores the n most recent passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd using the password hashing algorithm set in the pam_unix module. This allows the sha512 hashing algorithm to be used.
rules.impact: The Remember=n argument should be removed to ensure that a strong password hashing algorithm is used. A stronger hash provides additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine old local user passwords stored in /etc/security/opasswd.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: A cryptographic hash function transforms input of arbitrary length into a fixed-length output. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password, converting it into another string called a hashed password.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 and Yescrypt algorithms provide a stronger hash than other algorithms used by Linux to generate password hashes. A stronger hash provides additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine local user passwords. Note: These changes apply only to the local system.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok — during a password change, force the module to set the new password to the one provided by a previously stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: Password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to force passwords to expire after they reach a certain age. PASS_MAX_DAYS <N> is the maximum number of days a password may be used. If the password is older than this, a password change will be forced. If not specified, -1 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: The window of opportunity for an attacker to use compromised credentials or to successfully compromise credentials via an online brute-force attack is limited by the password expiration period. Therefore, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity. We recommend changing passwords annually. This is primarily because, despite good intentions, users will share credentials across accounts. Thus, even if a breach is publicly disclosed, the user may not see that notice or may forget they have an account on that site. This can leave shared credentials vulnerable indefinitely. Having an organizational policy that requires password expiration within 1 year (annually) is a reasonable compromise to mitigate this issue with minimal user burden. Page 668

rules.title: The minimum number of days for a password is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MIN_DAYS <N> is the minimum number of days allowed between password changes. Any attempt to change the password before that time is rejected. If not specified, the value 0 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe the chosen password is protected against compromise. Unfortunately, passwords are compromised, and if an attacker targets a specific individual user's account, then, with prior knowledge about that user, reuse of old, potentially compromised passwords may lead to a security breach. By restricting how frequently a password can be changed, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls.

rules.title: A password expiration warning is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days. PASS_WARN_AGE <N> is the number of days a warning is issued before password expiration. Zero means the warning is issued only on the day of expiration; a negative value means no warning is issued. If not specified, no warning is issued.
rules.impact: Advance warning of password expiration gives users time to think of a secure password. Users caught by surprise may choose a simple password or write it down where it can be discovered.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: A cryptographic hash function transforms input of arbitrary length into output of fixed length. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password, turning it into another string called a hashed password. ENCRYPT_METHOD (string) — defines the system default password encryption algorithm (if no algorithm is specified on the command line). It may take one of the following values: • MD5 — an MD5-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password • SHA256 — a SHA256-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password • SHA512 — a SHA512-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password • BCRYPT — a BCRYPT-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password • YESCRYPT — a YESCRYPT-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password • DES — a DES-based algorithm will be used to encrypt the password (default). Notes: • This parameter overrides the legacy MD5_CRYPT_ENAB variable. • This parameter affects only the creation of group passwords. • Generation of user passwords is performed by PAM and depends on the PAM configuration. • It is recommended that this variable be set in accordance with the PAM configuration.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 and Yescrypt algorithms provide a stronger hash than other algorithms used by Linux to generate password hashes. A stronger hash provides additional system protection by increasing the level of effort required for an attacker to successfully determine local group passwords. Page 677

rules.title: Inactive password lockout is configured
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period of time can be disabled automatically. INACTIVE defines the number of days after the password maximum lifetime is reached during which the user must replace that password. The value is stored in the shadow password file. Entering 0 will disable an expired password without delay. Entering -1 will clear the corresponding field in the shadow password file.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a system security threat because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: The last password change date for all users is in the past
rules.explanation: All users must have a password change date in the past.
rules.impact: If a user's recorded password change date is in the future, the user may bypass the configured password expiration.

rules.title: Root is the only account with UID 0
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
rules.impact: This access should be restricted to the root account by default and only from the system console. Administrative access should be performed through an unprivileged account using an approved mechanism, as specified in the recommendation "Ensure that access to the su command is restricted".

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root account belongs to. This affects access rights to files created by the root account.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent unprivileged users from accidentally accessing files owned by root.

rules.title: The root group is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: The groupmod command can be used to specify which group the root group belongs to. This affects permissions on files owned by the root group.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root group helps prevent accidental access by unprivileged users to files owned by the root group.

rules.title: Access to the root account is controlled
rules.explanation: There are several ways to access the root account directly. Without a password set, any user can gain access and thereby control the entire system.
rules.impact: Access to root must always be protected.

rules.title: Root path integrity
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command on the system and can be tricked into unintentionally running a program if PATH is set incorrectly.
rules.impact: Including the current working directory (.) or another writable directory in the root user's executable path increases the likelihood that an attacker can gain superuser access by causing an administrator operating as root to execute a Trojan horse program. Page 693

rules.title: The root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. The mask is not simply subtracted; it is processed bitwise. Bits set in the umask are cleared in the resulting file mode. umask may be set with octal or symbolic values: • Octal (numeric) value — represented by three or four digits, e.g. umask 0027 or umask 027. If a four-digit mask is used, the first digit is ignored. The remaining three digits affect the resulting permissions for user, group, and world/other respectively. • Symbolic value — represented by a comma-separated list for user u, group g, and world/other o. The listed permissions are not masked by umask. For example, a mask set with umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is the symbolic equivalent of octal mask 027. This mask will set a newly created directory with file mode drwxr-x--- and a newly created file with file mode rw-r-----. Root user shell configuration files: • /root/.bash_profile — executed to configure the root user shell before the initial command prompt is started. Read only by login shells. • /root/.bashrc — executed for interactive shells; read only by a shell that is both interactive and non-login. umask is applied according to precedence. If umask is set in multiple locations, this order of precedence determines the default umask on the system. Precedence order: 1. /root/.bash_profile 2. /root/.bashrc 3. System default mask Page 696
rules.impact: Setting a secure umask value ensures that users make a deliberate choice of file access permissions. A permissive umask value may result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: Most distributions include a number of accounts that are used to manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell. In addition, a user may add special accounts that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that accounts not used by regular users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell. By default, most distributions set an invalid string in the password field for these accounts, but it is also recommended that the shell field in the password file be set to the nologin shell. This prevents the account from potentially being used to run any commands.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Most distributions include a number of accounts that are used to manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell. In addition, a user may add special accounts that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that accounts not used by regular users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell. By default, most distributions set an invalid string in the password field for these accounts, but it is also recommended that the shell field in the password file be set to the nologin shell. This prevents the account from potentially being used to run any commands.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file that contains the full path names of valid login shells. This file is used by the chsh command and is available for query by other programs. Be aware that some programs consult this file to determine whether a user is a regular user; for example, FTP daemons traditionally deny access to users whose shells are not listed in this file.
rules.impact: A user can use chsh to change the configured shell. If a user is configured with a shell that is not listed in /etc/shells, the system assumes the account is restricted in some way. For chsh, this means the user cannot change that value. Other programs may query this list and apply similar restrictions. By placing nologin in /etc/shells, any user whose shell is nologin is treated as a full, unrestricted user. This is not the expected behavior for nologin.

rules.title: The default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: TMOUT is an environment setting that defines the shell timeout in seconds. • TMOUT=n — sets the shell timeout to n seconds. Setting TMOUT=0 disables the timeout. • readonly TMOUT — sets the TMOUT environment variable as read-only, preventing unwanted changes at runtime. • Export TMOUT — exports the TMOUT variable. System-wide shell configuration files: • /etc/profile — used to set system-wide environment variables in user shells. Sometimes the variables are the same as in the .bash_profile file; however, this file is used to set the initial PATH or PS1 for all system shell users. It is executed only for interactive login shells or shells invoked with the --login option. • /etc/profile.d — /etc/profile will execute scripts from /etc/profile.d/*.sh. It is recommended to place your configuration in a shell script in /etc/profile.d to set your own system-wide environment variables. • /etc/bashrc — the system-wide version of .bashrc. On Fedora-derived distributions, /etc/bashrc also sources /etc/profile.d/*.sh if the shell is not a login shell, but redirects output to /dev/null if it is non-interactive. It is executed only for interactive shells or if BASH_ENV is set to /etc/bashrc.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access to another user's shell session that was left unattended. It also terminates an idle session and frees resources associated with that session.

rules.title: The default user mask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). umask changes the Linux default permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. The mask is not simply subtracted; it is processed bitwise. Bits that are set in umask are cleared in the resulting file mode. umask can be set with octal or symbolic values: • Octal (numeric) value — represented by three or four digits, e.g. umask 0027 or umask 027. If a four-digit mask is used, the first digit is ignored. The remaining three digits affect the resulting permissions for user, group, and world/other respectively. • Symbolic value — represented by a comma-separated list for user u, group g, and world/other o. The listed permissions are not masked by umask. For example, a mask set with umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is the symbolic equivalent of octal mask 027. This mask will set a newly created directory to file mode drwxr-x--- and a newly created file to file mode rw-r-----. The default mask can be configured using the pam_umask module or in a system-wide shell configuration file. A user who creates directories or files may, at their discretion, change permissions with the chmod command or choose a different default umask by adding a umask command to a user shell configuration file (.bash_profile or .bashrc) in their home directory. Page 710 Setting the default umask: • pam_umask module: o will set umask according to the system default in /etc/login.defs and user settings, addressing the problem of different umask settings for different shells, display managers, remote sessions, etc. o The umask=<mask> value in /etc/login.defs is interpreted as octal o Setting USERGROUPS_ENAB to yes in /etc/login.defs (the default): ▪ will allow the group umask bits to be set the same as the owner bits (examples: 022 -> 002, 077 -> 007) for non-root users if uid matches gid and the username matches <primary group name>. ▪ userdel will remove the user's group if it has no remaining members, and useradd will create a default group named after the user. • System-wide shell configuration file: o /etc/profile — used to set system-wide environment variables in user shells. Sometimes the variables are the same as in .bash_profile; however, this file is used to set the initial PATH or PS1 for all system shell users. It is executed only for interactive login shells or shells invoked with the --login option. o /etc/profile.d — /etc/profile will execute scripts from /etc/profile.d/*.sh. It is recommended to place your configuration in a shell script in /etc/profile.d to set your own system-wide environment variables. o /etc/bashrc — the system-wide version of .bashrc. On Fedora-derived distributions, /etc/bashrc also invokes /etc/profile.d/*.sh if the shell is not a login shell, but redirects output to /dev/null if it is non-interactive. It is executed only for interactive shells or if BASH_ENV is set to /etc/bashrc. User shell configuration files: • ~/.bash_profile — executed to configure the shell before the initial command prompt. Read only by login shells. • ~/.bashrc — executed for interactive shells; read only by a shell that is both interactive and non-login. umask is applied in priority order. If umask is set in multiple places, this priority order determines the system default umask. Page 711 Priority order: 1. A file in /etc/profile.d/ ending in .sh — this overrides any other system-wide umask setting 2. In /etc/profile 3. In the pam_umask.so module in /etc/pam.d/postlogin 4. In /etc/login.defs 5. In /etc/default/login
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask ensures that users make a conscious choice about file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users. Page 712

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE) is an intrusion detection tool that uses predefined rules to verify the integrity of files and directories on a Linux operating system. AIDE has its own database for verifying the integrity of files and directories. AIDE takes snapshots of files and directories, including modification time, permissions, and file hashes, which can then be used to compare against the current state of the file system to detect changes on the system.
rules.impact: By monitoring file system state, compromised files can be detected to prevent or limit the impact of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or modified binaries.

rules.title: File system integrity is checked regularly
rules.explanation: Periodic file system integrity checking is required to detect changes in the file system.
rules.impact: Periodic file integrity checking allows the system administrator to regularly determine whether critical files have been modified in an unauthorized manner.

rules.title: Cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open-source audit tools required to successfully view and manage audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting the integrity of tools used for auditing is an important step toward ensuring the integrity of audit information. Audit information includes all information (for example, audit records, audit settings, and audit reports) needed to successfully audit information system activity. Attackers may replace audit tools or inject code into existing tools in order to hide or remove system activity from audit logs. Audit tools should be cryptographically signed so that it is possible to determine when audit tools have been altered, manipulated, or replaced. An example is a checksum hash of a file or files.

rules.title: The Journald service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The systemd-journald service is enabled and can capture log events.
rules.impact: If the systemd-journald service is not allowed to start at boot, the system will not record logging events.

rules.title: Access to the Journald log file is configured
rules.explanation: Journald will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. This parameter determines which permissions will be applied to newly created files.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions to enable archiving and protection of sensitive data. Page 733

rules.title: Journald log file rotation is configured
rules.explanation: Journald includes the ability to rotate log files regularly to avoid filling the system with logs or allowing logs to grow unmanageably. The file /etc/systemd/journald.conf is a configuration file used to specify the rotation order of logs created by Journald.
rules.impact: By keeping log files smaller and more manageable, the system administrator can easily archive these files to another system and spend less time reviewing excessively large log files.

rules.title: Only one logging system is in use
rules.explanation: Best practices recommend using a single centralized logging system to manage logs. Choose one service, either rsyslog — OR — Journald, to be used as the single centralized logging system.
rules.impact: Configuring only one logging service (rsyslog — OR — Journald) avoids redundancy, optimizes resources, simplifies configuration and management, and ensures consistency.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote supports sending the journal events it collects to a remote journal host or receiving messages from remote hosts, which enables centralized log management.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload authentication is configured
rules.explanation: Journald systemd-journal-upload supports sending the journal events it collects to a remote journal host.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: Journald systemd-journal-upload supports sending the journal events it collects to a remote journal host.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote journald supports receiving messages from remote hosts, thereby acting as a log server. Clients should not receive data from other hosts. Note: • The same systemd-journal-remote package is used both to send logs to remote hosts and to receive incoming logs. • For receiving logs, there are two services: systemd-journal-remote.socket and systemd-journal-remote.service.
rules.impact: If the client is configured to receive data, thereby turning it into a server, the client system operates outside its operational boundaries. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: ForwardToSyslog logging is disabled
rules.explanation: Journal data must be retained within the service and must not be forwarded to other services.
rules.impact: IF Journald is the log collection method, all system logs should be processed by Journald and not forwarded to other logging mechanisms. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: Journald Compress is configured
rules.explanation: The Journald system includes the ability to compress files that are too large to avoid filling the system with logs or allowing log size to become unmanageable.
rules.impact: Uncompressed large files can unexpectedly fill the file system, resulting in resource unavailability. Compressing logs before writing can prevent sudden and unexpected impact on the file system. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: Journald Storage is configured
rules.explanation: Log data may be stored in volatile memory or locally on the server. In-memory logs are lost on system reboot. By storing logs on the server's local disk, they are protected from loss due to reboot.
rules.impact: Writing log data to disk will provide the ability for forensic recovery of events that may have affected system operation or security, even after a crash or reboot. Note: This recommendation applies only if Journald is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if rsyslog is used.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog software is recommended in environments where Journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transmission (i.e., TCP), the ability to log in database formats, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package. Note: This recommendation applies only if rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if Journald is used.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: After installing the rsyslog package, ensure that the service is enabled.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not permitted to start at boot, the system will not record logging events. Note: This recommendation applies only when rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if Journald is used.

rules.title: Journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: Data from systemd-journald can be stored in volatile memory or locally on the server. Utilities exist to remotely export systemd-journald logs; however, using the rsyslog service provides a consistent means of collecting and exporting logs.
rules.impact: - IF - rsyslog is the preferred method of log collection, all system logs should be sent to it for further processing.

rules.title: The rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: rsyslog will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. The $FileCreateMode parameter allows you to specify the creation mode in which rsyslog creates new files. If not specified, the value 0644 is used (which preserves backward compatibility with earlier releases). The specified value should always be a four-digit octal number whose leading digit is zero. Note that the actual permission depends on the rsyslogd process umask. $FileCreateMode can be specified multiple times. If so, it defines the creation mode for all selector lines that follow until the next $FileCreateMode parameter. The order of the lines is vital.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions so that sensitive data is archived and protected. Note: This recommendation applies only if rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if systemd-journald is used.

rules.title: Rsyslog logging is configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf define logging rules and the files that should be used to record certain classes of messages.
rules.impact: A large amount of important security-related information is sent through rsyslog (for example, successful and failed su attempts, failed logon attempts, root logon attempts, and so on). Note: This recommendation applies only if rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if Journald is used.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: rsyslog supports sending collected log events to a remote log host or receiving messages from remote hosts, which enables centralized log management.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can tamper with or delete log data stored on the local system. Note: This recommendation applies only if the rsyslog method is selected for client-side logging. Do not apply this recommendation if systemd-journald is used. Page 774

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from a remote client
rules.explanation: rsyslog supports receiving messages from remote hosts, thereby acting as a log server. Clients must not receive data from other hosts.
rules.impact: If a client is configured to receive data, thereby turning it into a server, the client system operates outside its operational boundaries. Note: This recommendation applies only if rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if systemd-journald is used.

rules.title: Rsyslog logrotate is configured
rules.explanation: The system includes the ability to rotate log files regularly to avoid filling the system with logs or allowing logs to grow unmanageably. The file /etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog is a configuration file used to rotate log files created by rsyslog.
rules.impact: By keeping log files smaller and more manageable, the system administrator can more easily archive these files to another system and spend less time reviewing excessively large log files. Note: This recommendation applies only if rsyslog is selected as the client-side logging method. Do not apply this recommendation if systemd-journald is used. Page 779

rules.title: Access to all log files is configured
rules.explanation: Log files contain information from many local system services or, in the case of a centralized log server, also logs from other systems. Log files are typically located in /var/log/, although an application can be configured to store logs elsewhere. If your application stores logs in another location, be sure to run the same test at that location.
rules.impact: It is important that log files have correct permissions to ensure sensitive data is protected and that only appropriate users/groups have access to them.

rules.title: Audit packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Logging of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: Auditing of processes that start before audit is enabled
rules.explanation: grub2 is configured so that auditable processes can be audited even if they start before Auditd starts.
rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before audit so that potentially malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: Audit_backlog_limit is sufficient
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit parameter determines how many audit records can be stored in the audit log. The default value of 64 may be insufficient to store all audit events during boot.
rules.impact: If audit=1 during boot, the backlog will contain 64 entries. If more than 64 entries are created during boot, Auditd records will be lost and potential malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The Auditd daemon is enabled to record system events.
rules.impact: Logging of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The maximum audit log file size is configured. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is created.
rules.impact: It is important to define an appropriate log file size so that logs do not impact the system or lose audit data.

rules.title: Audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter determines how to handle an audit log file that reaches the maximum size. The Keep_logs value will rotate logs but never delete old logs.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the storage costs.

rules.title: The system shuts down when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon can be configured to halt the system or place the system in single-user mode if there is no free space or an error is detected on the partition containing the audit log files. The disk_full_action parameter tells the system what action to take if there is no free space on the partition containing the audit log files. Valid values: ignore, syslog, rotate, exec, suspend, single, and halt. • ignore — the audit daemon will issue a syslog message, but no other action will be taken • syslog — the audit daemon will issue a warning to syslog • rotate — the audit daemon will rotate logs, discarding the oldest to free space • exec — /path-to-script will execute a script. You cannot pass parameters to the script. The script is also responsible for telling the auditd daemon to resume logging after it completes its action. • suspend — the audit daemon will stop writing records to disk; Valid values: ignore, syslog, exec, suspend, single, and halt. • ignore — the audit daemon will take no action • syslog — the audit daemon will issue no more than 5 consecutive warnings to syslog • exec — /path-to-script will execute a script. You cannot pass parameters to the script • suspend — the audit daemon will stop writing records to disk • single — the audit daemon will place the computer system in single-user mode • halt — the audit daemon will halt the system
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the risk of failing to detect unauthorized access or non-repudiation outweighs the benefit of system availability. Page 808

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs have insufficient space
rules.explanation: The audit daemon can be configured to halt the system, put the system into single-user mode, or send a warning message if there is insufficient space in the partition containing the audit log files. The space_left_action parameter tells the system which action to take if the system has detected that the disk is beginning to run out of space. Valid values are ignore, syslog, rotate, email, exec, suspend, single, and halt. • ignore, the audit daemon does nothing • syslog, the audit daemon issues a warning to syslog • rotate, the audit daemon will rotate logs, discarding the oldest to free space • email, the audit daemon will send a warning to the email account specified in action_mail_acct and will also send a message to syslog • exec, /path-to-script will execute a script. You cannot pass parameters to the script. The script is also responsible for telling the auditd daemon to resume logging after it has completed its action • suspend, the audit daemon will stop writing records to disk; Valid values are ignore, syslog, rotate, email, exec, suspend, single, and halt. • ignore, the audit daemon does nothing • syslog, the audit daemon issues a warning to syslog • rotate, the audit daemon will rotate logs, discarding the oldest to free space • email, the audit daemon will send a warning to the email account specified in action_mail_acct and will also send a message to syslog • exec, /path-to-script will execute a script. You cannot pass parameters to the script.
