The script is also responsible for instructing the audit daemon to resume logging after it has completed its action. • suspend, the audit daemon will stop writing records to disk. • single, the audit daemon will put the computer system into single-user mode. • halt, the audit daemon will shut down the system.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the need to detect unauthorized access or ensure non-repudiation outweighs the benefit of system availability.

rules.title: Changes in the system administration scope (sudoers) are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system is correctly configured and forces system administrators to log in under their own names first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, scope changes can be monitored. The /etc/sudoers file or files in /etc/sudoers.d will be written if the file(s) or related attributes change. Audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".
rules.impact: Changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d may indicate that an unauthorized change has been made to the system administrator's scope of activity. Page 815

rules.title: Actions of another user are always logged
rules.explanation: sudo provides users with temporary elevated privileges to perform operations as the superuser or another user.
rules.impact: Creating an audit log of users with temporarily elevated privileges and the operations they performed is essential for reporting. Administrators will want to correlate events recorded in the audit log with entries recorded in the sudo log file to verify whether unauthorized commands were executed. Page 818

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor the sudo log file. If the system has been properly configured to disable use of the su command and force all administrators to log in first and then use sudo to execute privileged commands, then all administrator commands will be recorded in /var/log/sudo.log. Each time a command is executed, an audit event will be initiated because the /var/log/sudo.log file will be opened for writing, and the executed administrative command will be written to the log.
rules.impact: Changes to /var/log/sudo.log indicate that an administrator executed a command or that the log file itself was tampered with. Administrators will need to correlate events recorded in the audit log with entries in /var/log/sudo.log to verify whether unauthorized commands were executed. Page 822

rules.title: Events that modify date and time information are collected
rules.explanation: Capture events in which the system date and/or time were changed. The parameters in this section are set to determine whether: • adjtimex - adjust the kernel clock • settimeofday - set the time using timeval and timezone structures • stime - use seconds since 01.01.1970 • clock_settime - allow setting of multiple internal clocks and timers when system calls are executed. In addition, on exit, always write an audit record to the configured audit log file, tagging the records with a unique identifier such as "time-change".
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may indicate malicious activity on the system. Page 826

rules.title: Events that modify the system network environment are collected
rules.explanation: Record changes to network environment files or system calls. The following parameters watch the following system calls and record an audit event when the system call exits: • sethostname — set the system hostname • setdomainname — set the system domain name. Watched files: • /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net — messages displayed before login • /etc/hosts — file containing hostnames and associated IP addresses • /etc/hostname — file containing the system hostname • /etc/sysconfig/network — additional information valid for all network interfaces. • /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ — directory containing network interface scripts and configuration files. • /etc/NetworkManager/ — directory containing configuration files and settings used by NetworkManager.
rules.impact: Monitoring sethostname and setdomainname will identify potential unauthorized changes to the system's host and domain names. Changing these names could potentially disrupt security settings established based on those names. The /etc/hosts file is monitored for changes that may indicate an unauthorized attacker is attempting to alter computer-to-IP address associations and trick users and processes into connecting to unintended machines. Monitoring /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net is important because attackers may place disinformation in these files and trick users into providing information to the attacker. Monitoring /etc/sysconfig/network is important because it can show whether network interfaces or scripts are being changed in a way that could make the machine unavailable or compromised. All audit records should have an appropriate tag associated with them. Page 830

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: Monitor privileged programs, those that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution, to determine whether unprivileged users are executing these commands.
rules.impact: Execution of privileged commands by unprivileged users may indicate that someone is attempting to gain unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor unsuccessful file access attempts. The following parameters are associated with system calls that manage files: • create – creat • open – open, openat • truncate – truncate, ftruncate An audit log record will be written only if all of the following criteria are met for the user when attempting to access a file: • unprivileged user (auid>=UID_MIN) • not a daemon event (auid=4294967295/unset/-1) • if the system call returned EACCES (access denied) or EPERM (another persistent error associated with the specific system call)
rules.impact: Failed attempts to open, create, or truncate files may indicate that a person or process is attempting to obtain unauthorized access to the system. Page 838

rules.title: Events that modify user/group information are collected
rules.explanation: Record events that affect changes to user or group information, including passwords and old passwords if they are used. • /etc/group – system groups • /etc/passwd – system users • /etc/gshadow – encrypted password for each group • /etc/shadow – system user passwords • /etc/security/opasswd – store of old passwords if the corresponding PAM module is used • /etc/nsswitch.conf – file that configures the system's use of various databases and name-resolution mechanisms • /etc/pam.conf – file that defines the authentication services used and the order in which services are used. • /etc/pam.d — directory contains PAM configuration files for each PAM-aware application. The options in this section will monitor the files to determine whether they were opened for writing or had attribute changes (for example, permissions) and will tag them with the identity identifier in the audit log file.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to these files may indicate that the system is compromised and that an unauthorized user is attempting to conceal their activity or compromise additional accounts. Page 842

rules.title: Events that change discretionary access control permissions are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor changes to file access permissions, attributes, owners, and groups. The options in this section monitor changes to system calls that affect file permissions and attributes. The following commands and system calls affect permissions, ownership, and various file attributes. • chmod • fchmod • fchmodat • chown • fchown • fchownat • lchown • setxattr • lsetxattr • fsetxattr • removexattr • lremovexattr • fremovexattr In all cases, an audit record will be written only for non-system user IDs and will ignore daemon events. All audit records will be tagged with the identifier "perm_mod".
rules.impact: Monitoring file attribute changes can alert a system administrator to activity that may indicate attacker activity or a policy violation. Page 846

rules.title: Successful file system mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor use of the mount system call. The mount (and umount) system call controls mounting and unmounting of file systems. The options below configure the system to generate an audit record when the mount system call is used by an unprivileged user.
rules.impact: It is highly unusual for an unprivileged user to mount filesystems on the system. Although tracking mount commands gives the system administrator evidence that external media may have been mounted (based on inspecting the mount source and confirming the type of external media), it does not conclusively indicate that data was exported to the media. System administrators who wish to determine whether data was exported will also need to track successful open, creat, and truncate system calls that require write access to a file at the mount point of the external media filesystem. This can serve as a reliable indication that a write occurred. The only way to truly prove this is to track successful writes to the external media. Tracking write system calls can quickly fill the audit log and is not recommended. Guidance on configuration parameters for tracking data export to media is beyond the scope of this document. Page 851

rules.title: Session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Monitor session initiation events. The settings in this section monitor changes to files associated with session events. • /var/run/utmp — tracks all logged-in users. • /var/log/wtmp — the file tracks logon, logoff, shutdown, and reboot events. • /var/log/btmp — tracks failed logon attempts. It can be read by entering the command /usr/bin/last -f /var/log/btmp. All audit records will be tagged with the identifier "session".
rules.impact: Monitoring these files for changes can alert the system administrator to logons at unusual hours, which may indicate attacker activity (i.e., a user logging on at a time when they do not normally log on). Page 855

rules.title: Login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor logon and logoff events. The parameters below track changes to files related to logon/logoff events. • /var/log/lastlog — retains records of the user's last successful logon. • /var/run/faillock — directory stores failed logon records from the pam_faillock module.
rules.impact: Monitoring logon/logoff events can provide the system administrator with information related to brute-force attacks against user logons. Page 859

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor the use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes. This configuration statement sets monitoring for: • unlink — delete a file • unlinkat — delete a file attribute • rename — rename a file • renameat — rename a file attribute — system calls and tags them with the identifier "delete".
rules.impact: Monitoring these calls from unprivileged users can provide the system administrator with evidence that improper deletion of files and file attributes associated with protected files is occurring. Although this audit option will check all events, system administrators will need to look for specific privileged files that are deleted or modified. Page 862

rules.title: Events that change mandatory access control on the system are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor SELinux, an implementation of mandatory access control. The options below monitor any write access (possible addition, deletion, or modification of files in the directory) or attribute changes in the /etc/selinux/ and /usr/share/selinux/ directories. Note: If another mandatory access control method is used, changes to the corresponding directories must be audited.
rules.impact: File changes in the /etc/selinux/ and /usr/share/selinux/ directories may indicate that an unauthorized user is attempting to alter access controls and security contexts, resulting in system compromise. Page 866

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the chcon command.
rules.impact: The chcon command is used to change the security context of a file. Without generating audit records that meet the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate events related to an incident, or to determine those responsible. Audit records may be generated by various information system components (for example, a module or a policy filter). Page 869

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the setfacl command.
rules.impact: This utility sets access control lists (ACLs) for files and directories. Without generating audit records that meet the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate events related to an incident or to determine who is responsible. Audit records can be generated from various information system components (for example, a module or policy filter). Page 873

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the chacl command. chacl is an IRIX compatibility command and is supported for users who are familiar with its use from XFS or IRIX.
rules.impact: chacl modifies the ACL for a file or directory. Without generating audit records that meet the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine who is responsible. Audit records can be generated from various information system components (for example, a module or policy filter). Page 877

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the usermod command.
rules.impact: The usermod command modifies system account files to reflect changes specified on the command line. Without generating audit records that meet the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate events related to an incident or to determine those responsible. Audit records can be generated from various information system components (for example, a module or a policy filter). Page 881

rules.title: Kernel module load, unload, and modification are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor loading and unloading of kernel modules. All module loading/listing/dependency checking is performed by kmod via symbolic links. The following system calls control loading and unloading of modules: • init_module – load a module • finit_module – load a module (used when the overhead of using cryptographically signed modules to determine module authenticity can be avoided) • delete_module – unload a module • create_module – create a loadable module entry • query_module – query the kernel for various bits related to modules. Any execution of module load and unload programs and system calls will generate an audit record with the modules identifier.
rules.impact: Monitoring the use of all the various methods of manipulating kernel modules can provide system administrators with evidence that an unauthorized change was made to a kernel module, which may compromise system security. Page 885

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: System auditing is configured so that audit rules cannot be modified using auditctl. Setting the "-e 2" flag places auditing into immutable mode. Audit changes can be made only when the system is rebooted. Note: This setting will require a system reboot to update the active auditd configuration settings.
rules.impact: In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot modify the audit system to potentially conceal malicious activity and then restore the audit rules. Users are likely to notice a system reboot, which can alert administrators to an attempt to make unauthorized audit changes.

rules.title: The running and on-disk configurations are the same
rules.explanation: The audit system has both a disk and a running configuration. These configuration settings may differ. Note: Due to limitations of augenrules and Auditctl, there is no absolute guarantee that loading rule sets with augenrules --load will load all rules or even that the user will be informed if a problem occurred while loading rules.
rules.impact: Differences in configuration between what is currently running and what is on disk can cause unexpected problems or create a false impression of compliance.

rules.title: The audit log file directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: The audit log directory contains audit log files.
rules.impact: Audit information includes all information, including audit records, audit settings, and audit reports. This information is required for successful auditing of system activity. This information must be protected from unauthorized modification or deletion. If this information is compromised, forensic analysis cannot be performed and the true source of potentially malicious system activity cannot be identified. Page 895

rules.title: The audit log file mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and its activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising their confidentiality. Page 898

rules.title: The owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and its activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising their confidentiality. Page 901

rules.title: The audit log file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and its activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising their confidentiality. Page 904

rules.title: Audit configuration file mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control Auditd and the events that are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files may allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent auditing of critical events or affect system performance due to audit log overflow. Incorrect configuration of audit configuration files may also make it difficult to establish and investigate events related to an incident.

rules.title: The owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control Auditd and the events that are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files may allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent auditing of critical events or affect system performance due to audit log overflow. Incorrect configuration of audit configuration files may also make it difficult to establish and investigate events related to an incident.

rules.title: The group owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control Auditd and the events that are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files may allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent auditing of critical events or affect system performance due to audit log overflow. Incorrect configuration of audit configuration files may also make it difficult to establish and investigate events related to an incident.

rules.title: The audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open-source audit tools required to successfully view and manage audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manage log data. Protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operations on audit information. Page 913

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for those utilities to function.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect the /etc/passwd file from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/passwd- from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/group are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains the list of all valid groups defined on the system. The command below provides read/write access for root and read access for everyone else.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users, but must remain readable because this information is used in many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group- file contains a backup list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect the /etc/group- file from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, for example the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them. Other security information stored in the /etc/shadow file (for example, expiration dates) may also be useful for compromising user accounts.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow- file is used to store backup user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/shadow- from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to the /etc/gshadow file, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them. Other security information stored in the /etc/gshadow file (for example, group administrator information) may also be useful for compromising a group.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow- file is used to store backup group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as hashed passwords and other security information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/gshadow- from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file containing the full names of valid login shells. This file is used by the chsh command and is available for query by other programs.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect the /etc/shells file from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/security/opasswd are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/security/opasswd and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old contain previous user passwords if the system uses pam_unix or pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect the /etc/security/opasswd file from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or as a result of malicious activity.

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are secured
rules.explanation: World-writable files are the least secure. Data in writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World-writable files can also indicate a poorly written script or program that could potentially cause a more serious system integrity breach. For additional information, see the chmod(2) man page. Setting the sticky bit on world-writable directories prevents users from deleting or renaming files in that directory that they do not own.
rules.impact: Data in writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World-writable files may also indicate a poorly written script or program that could potentially cause a more serious integrity compromise of the system. This feature prevents files in writable directories (for example, /tmp) that are owned by another user from being deleted or renamed.

rules.title: Files or directories without an owner and group do not exist
rules.explanation: Administrators may remove users or groups from the system and not remove all files and/or directories owned by those users or groups.
rules.impact: A new user or group assigned the user ID or group ID of a deleted user may ultimately become the owner of the deleted user or group's files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are audited
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for using an SUID or SGID program is to allow users to perform functions (for example, changing a password) that require root privileges.
rules.impact: There are legitimate reasons for SUID and SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the audit action and check whether system binaries have a checksum that differs from the package checksum. This indicates that the binary may have been replaced. rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts can use shadowed passwords. When shadowed passwords are used, passwords are stored in the shadow password file /etc/shadow, encrypted with a salted one-way hash. Accounts with a shadowed password have an x in the second field of the /etc/passwd file.
rules.impact: The /etc/passwd file also contains information such as user and group identifiers that are used by many system programs. Therefore, the /etc/passwd file must remain world-readable. Even though the password is encoded with a randomly generated one-way hash function, an attacker can still crack it if they gain access to the /etc/passwd file. This can be mitigated by using shadow passwords, thereby moving passwords from the /etc/passwd file to /etc/shadow. The /etc/shadow file is configured so that only root can read and write it. This helps reduce the risk of an attacker obtaining encoded passwords to conduct a dictionary attack. Note: • All accounts should have passwords or be locked to prevent use of the account by an unauthorized user. • A user account with an empty second field in the /etc/passwd file allows login to the account by specifying only the username.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field means anyone can log on as that user without specifying a password.
rules.impact: All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent use of the account by an unauthorized user.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Over time, errors and system administration changes can result in groups being defined in /etc/passwd rather than in /etc/group.
rules.impact: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group permissions are not managed properly.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate user identifier (UID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure accountability and to provide appropriate access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group identifier (GID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change the GID field.
rules.impact: User groups should be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protection.

rules.title: Duplicate user names do not exist
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change a username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create files with the first UID for that username and access them in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: Duplicate group names do not exist
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group name, an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change a group name.
rules.impact: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create files with the first GID for that group and gain access to them in /etc/group. Essentially, the GID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: A user's home directory is space defined for a specific user to set local environment variables and store personal files. Although a system administrator can set secure permissions on user home directories, users can easily reverse them. Users may be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory, or with a home directory that does not actually exist.
rules.impact: Because the user is responsible for files stored in the user's home directory, the user should own that directory. Group-writable or world-writable user home directories may allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges. If a user's home directory does not exist or is not assigned, the user will be placed in "/" and will be unable to write any files or set local environment variables.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dotfiles is configured
rules.explanation: Although a system administrator can set secure permissions on users' "dot" files, users can easily override them. • The .forward file specifies the email address to which the user's mail will be forwarded. • The .rhosts file contains a "remote authentication" database for the rcp, rlogin, and rsh commands and the rcmd function. These files bypass the standard password-based user authentication mechanism. They define remote hosts and users that are considered trusted (that is, they are allowed access to the local system without providing a password). • The .netrc file contains credentials for logging in to a remote host or passing authentication via an API. • The .bash_history file tracks the user's commands.
rules.impact: User configuration files with excessive or incorrect access can allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.
